Endeavor

/en-DEV-er/ — accent on DEV · noun

Hear It

What It Means

An endeavor is a serious effort or attempt to accomplish something difficult.

Building the school library from donations alone was an ambitious endeavor.

Worked Example

A group of teenagers decides to build a community garden on an abandoned lot. Over a year, they clear the land, build raised beds, establish a watering system, and teach other kids to garden. Their ambitious endeavor transforms the neighborhood.

'Endeavor' is perfect here because it captures both the difficulty and the seriousness of the multi-year project. 'Effort' alone is too plain—it doesn't convey how challenging this was. 'Project' is close, but 'endeavor' emphasizes that it was a serious, difficult pursuit.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

effort: energy spent trying to accomplish something

attempt: a single try at doing something

quest: a long, dedicated search or mission

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

idleness: avoiding work, activity, or effort altogether

inaction: failure to act or make any attempt

Where it sits · how ambitious and demanding the undertaking — chore → task → project → endeavor

chore vs. endeavor: A chore sits far below an endeavor: a chore is a small, routine job like washing dishes, while an endeavor is a serious attempt at something genuinely difficult.

task vs. endeavor: A task is weaker than an endeavor: a task is a single defined piece of work, while an endeavor is a sustained, ambitious effort toward a hard goal.

project vs. endeavor: A project comes close to an endeavor but stops short: a project has a plan and an end date, while an endeavor carries a greater sense of striving and difficulty.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — en-

Prefix — en-: in, into (to put into) (Old French)

Root — deavor

Root — deavor: duty (from Old French devoir, 'duty,' from Latin debere, 'to owe'; respelled -deavor in English)

Put it together

Put it together: En- ('in, into') + deavor ('duty,' the Old French word devoir respelled in English, from Latin debere, 'to owe'): endeavor comes from the Old French phrase mettre en devoir, 'to put oneself in duty.' To endeavor is to make something your duty — a serious, committed effort to accomplish something difficult.

Use the root in a new word: debt

Use the root in a new word: debt: A debt is something you owe — from Latin debere, the same root behind the '-deavor' in endeavor, which began as a duty you owed yourself to carry out.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / neutral

Endeavor is the word for serious, difficult efforts that require commitment. If you mean casual work, say 'task' or 'job.' Use endeavor when the goal is genuinely challenging and worth mentioning—it gives the effort importance.
